query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the in‐situ formation of a brittle, phase‐selective oxide film in the eutectic microstructure becomes susceptible to mechanical removal during wear, exposing anodic phase boundaries that then undergo accelerated galvanic corrosion. The repetitive film removal and reformation creates a feedback loop that magnifies both wear and corrosion damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy comprising interwoven phases that differ in their oxidation tendencies and corrosion resistance, with one phase capable of forming a protective (but brittle) oxide layer at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous wear (controlled mechanical abrasion) and a corrosive environment at elevated temperatures, and compare it to tests where only wear or only corrosion are applied.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature conditions (around 800–900 °C) in an oxidizing and chloride-rich atmosphere, with a defined load and frequency for wear application.
generation.structural_mediator: An in-situ generated, brittle oxide film that forms preferentially on one phase; its integrity is compromised by mechanical wear, exposing underlying anodic regions at phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The elevated temperature promotes oxide formation that is not uniformly adherent across the different eutectic phases. During wear, the mechanically weak oxide is repeatedly removed, exposing anodic interfaces that, due to galvanic differences, corrode rapidly. This localized corrosion further weakens the microstructure, enhancing wear susceptibility and establishing a synergistic degradation process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to baseline conditions (wear only or corrosion only), samples under simultaneous wear and corrosion will display a significantly higher total degradation. Both the wear depth and the corrosion severity (e.g., higher corrosion current density) are expected to increase beyond an additive response, indicating a positive feedback loop between mechanical removal and corrosion attack.
generation.baseline: Identical alloy specimens tested under either wear-only or corrosion-only conditions at the same elevated temperature and corrosive atmosphere.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the ambient conditions are such that (a) temperature is sufficient to thermodynamically favor oxide formation (800–900 °C), (b) the environment provides adequate oxygen and chloride ions to enable aggressive, localized corrosion, and (c) the applied mechanical wear is high enough to remove the protective oxide intermittently without causing complete surface melting.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the synergistic acceleration of degradation and the exact contribution of galvanic effects versus mechanical oxide removal remain uncertain and may vary with small changes in alloy composition or test parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of identical eutectic HEA specimens and subject them to (a) wear-only, (b) corrosion-only, and (c) combined wear-corrosion conditions at 800–900 °C in a chloride-rich oxidizing atmosphere. Use identical mechanical load and duration for wear tests and standardized corrosion cells for the corrosive tests.
measurements: Total mass and volume loss (quantitative wear depth)
Corrosion current density via electrochemical measurements
Surface analyses (SEM/EDS and possibly in-situ imaging) to document oxide film integrity and distribution of corrosion damage at phase boundaries
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess passive film characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined wear-corrosion specimens do not exhibit a degradation rate (both in wear depth and corrosion metrics) that significantly exceeds the sum of the separate wear-only and corrosion-only conditions or if in-situ analyses show no evidence of cyclic oxide film removal and localized corrosion at phase boundaries, then the proposed synergistic mechanism is disproven.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA).
